extracted.intended_audience: young authors and poets (literary men) seeking guidance on poetic and dramatic diction and reception
extracted.subtask_description: Advice and critical maxims for writing and evaluating poetry and dramatic verse: diction, imagery, compounds, consistency of character-speech, effects of recitation and criticism, and the proper role of rules versus ends. Emphases include clarity, proportional causation in narrative, and prudence about publication and reception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule for admission of double epithets
rubrics_metrics.description: The rule for the admission of double epithets seems to be this: either that they should be already denizens of our language, such as blood-stained, terror-stricken, self-applauding: or when a new epithet, or one found in books only, is hazarded, that it, at least, be one word, not two words made one by mere virtue of the printers hyphen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: English is in its genius unfitted for compounds; if a writer, every time a compounded word suggests itself, would seek some other mode of expressing the same sense, he will likely find a better word. (Footnote example and Caesar’s advice are cited.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid translatable grandiloquence
rubrics_metrics.description: Whatever is translatable in other and simpler words of the same language, without loss of sense or dignity, is bad.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: N.B. 'dignity' here means absence of ludicrous and debasing associations. If a phrase can be rendered simply without loss, the original pomp is a fault.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer clarity over compounded/artificial diction
rubrics_metrics.description: A language almost without cases (English) is unfitted for many compounds; seek other modes of expression rather than force compound words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a new compounded epithet occurs, prefer finding an alternative phrasing or a single-word epithet; overuse of hyphenated compounds degrades diction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for reciter and audience effects on reception
rubrics_metrics.description: In calculating probable reception of a poem, subtract a large amount from the panegyric caused by recitation; the enkindling reciter lends his will and apprehensive faculty to auditors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allowances must be made for private enmity and for the necessity of a certain proportion of abuse/ridicule in reviews (to make them saleable). The temporary sympathy excited by a celebrated reciter can greatly exaggerate apparent merit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rules are means to ends; determine ends first
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules are but means to an end; consequently, where the ends are different, the rules must be likewise so. We must have ascertained what the end is before we can determine what the rules ought to be.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics err by treating rules as ends; e.g., the Greek stage rules were circumstances-driven, not universal prescriptions—Shakespeare’s different ends justify different rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency of imagery and character-voice
rubrics_metrics.description: Images and phrases used by a character should be consistent with that character’s established speech; singular, foreign, or borrowed images that appear unique and unrelated to other speech are senseless.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid senseless plagiarism or isolated images (e.g., spliced lines from Lear, Dryden, Milton) that do not fit the character; ensure metaphors and images arise organically from the character’s voice and situation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plausibility of character behavior and sudden transformations
rubrics_metrics.description: Sudden revolutions in a character’s manners (e.g., a youthful sinner metamorphosed into an old scold) that have no groundwork are outré and undermine credibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transformations should be motivated or signaled; unexplained shifts cause audiences to invent unlikely explanations and reduce dramatic effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative causation and proportionality
rubrics_metrics.description: There must be a sensible proportion between antecedents and consequents; the perception of cause and effect gives a substratum of permanence and identity to the flux of time and affords consolation to the afflicted soul.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readers find comfort in intelligible sequences; shapeless or unintelligible events magnify distress. Aim for clear causal relations in plotting and characterization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid bombast; preserve the visual likeness of similes
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not exaggerate or convert a clear visual simile into bombastic or absurd language that destroys the likeness (example: turning the Dog Star into a 'real dog' with fever-breath).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain the visual or analogical integrity of a simile; excessive exaggeration can render the image absurd and lose the intended effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious about translations that corrupt diction
rubrics_metrics.description: Translations (e.g., Pope’s Homer) can become the main source of pseudo-poetic diction and corrupt popular taste by substituting bombast or absurd phrasing for clear imagery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze translations sentence-by-sentence for fidelity of sense and propriety of diction; compare images to judge whether 'sense' or 'diction' is at fault.

rubrics_metrics.name: Autobiographical tone: avoid self-importance
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not open autobiographies with presumptuous or inflated claims such as 'The eventful life which I am about to record...'; such self-importance is ludicrous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Modesty in autobiographical tone is preferable; grandiose openings invite ridicule and undermine credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study exemplars but adapt their devices to context
rubrics_metrics.description: Authority of Milton and Shakespeare may be usefully pointed out to young authors, but note variation in their use of devices (e.g., Milton’s double epithets vs. Shakespeare’s restraint).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Learn from great authors, but do not imitate devices blindly; apply their techniques only where the ends and contexts match.
